messages.subject: [tlocoh-info] Sampling frequency graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,


I am new to tLoCoH and have a question about the sampling frequency graphs.
I have GPS tracking data for bilbies however there are some gaps and
missing data for the first part of my study (due to antenna breakages).
This means I only have 1-2 fixes per day for the first month, and then
several fixes per day for the following month (as the antennas were
repaired).



This then affects my sampling frequency graphs (example attached), and I am
concerned that the points at a low sampling frequency will affect the
temporal analyses. Should I consider trimming these data points using
â€œlxy.thin.byfreq()â€? Or is it best to keep them in?


Thanks in advance.



Kind regards,

Cass

messages.body_plain:
I think this is less about T-LoCoH and perhaps more about how to approach the analysis. T-LoCoHâ€™s strength is in using frequent data points to examine fine-scale temporal and spatial site use. I might be worthwhile to consider using a broad analysis for the two months based on 1 to 2 fixes per day (randomly choosing 1 to 2 data points in the second month) and the a finer scale analysis based on the second month of data (assuming you only have two months of data).

This suggestion of course is given without knowing what your questions are.

Damian

Damian C. Lidgard, PhD

Dalhousie University
Halifax, NS Canada

messages.subject: [tlocoh-info] Sampling frequency graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cassandra,

I agree with the answer by Damian Lidgard. As I understand it, you define a
"visit" period (in order to see whether 2 points in the same area is part
of a single visit or a revisit). Typically, for predators I used the
longest period they would stay on a single carcass. So if your sample
frequency is longer apart than the "visit period", there is no way to
classify it as anything else than a revisit. I would analyse the 2 periods
separately.

HTH.
Chavoux Luyt

messages.subject: [tlocoh-info] Sampling frequency graph
messages.body_plain:
I concur with Wayne, Chavoux and Damian. You can thin down the entire 
dataset to get a consistent ~2 pts per day, and analyze that subset for 
its spatial characteristics only (i.e., isopleths). In other words, 
ignore time when you construct hulls for this subset because the 
duration between observations is not meaningful (has less to do with the 
individual's behavior and more to do with noise from the sampling 
logistics). Then when you analyze the portion of the data that has a 
regular sampling frequency, you can include time when constructing 
hulls, compute hull metrics that assume enclosed points are near in 
space and time, construct metrics for revisitation, etc. Cheers, Andy
